summary: Cameroon routes almost every nationality through its official eVisa portal (evisacam.cm) — you apply online and the approved visa is issued on arrival or at an embassy — while citizens of fellow CEMAC states (Chad, CAR, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea) enter visa-free.

notes: Drones may not be brought in or flown without prior authorization from the Cameroonian authorities.
Export of ivory, protected wildlife products and unworked precious minerals is prohibited.

payments.text: Cash is essential. Cards work only at major hotels and some supermarkets in Douala and Yaoundé. ATMs exist in cities but can be unreliable; mobile money (MTN MoMo, Orange Money) is used everywhere for day-to-day payments.

safety.text: Most visits to Douala, Yaoundé and the coast are trouble-free, but governments advise against travel to the Far North (Boko Haram activity), the Northwest and Southwest regions (armed separatist conflict) and border areas with Chad and the Central African Republic. Petty crime and road accidents are the main everyday risks.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Cameroon travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to February — the main dry season — is best for the coast around Kribi, Mount Cameroon and the northern parks; heavy rains peak from July to October, especially in the south and west.

tips.text: Avoid the Northwest and Southwest (anglophone) regions, where an armed separatist conflict continues, and the Far North near Lake Chad — most governments advise against all travel to these areas.

Cameroon has moved visa issuance online: apply only on the official evisacam.cm portal and ignore third-party visa websites. The approved eVisa is issued on arrival at Douala, Yaoundé-Nsimalen or Garoua airports, or at an embassy.
Keep your yellow fever certificate with your passport. It is checked at the airport before you reach immigration, and you can be refused entry or vaccinated on the spot without it.
Avoid intercity road travel after dark — roads are poorly lit, breakdowns are common and there are frequent police checkpoints; carry your passport (or a certified copy) at all times.
Carry CFA franc cash and consider a local MTN or Orange SIM — mobile money is the easiest way to pay for taxis, markets and small hotels outside the big cities.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Cameroon?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes. Only citizens of the CEMAC bloc (Chad, Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea) enter visa-free; everyone else applies in advance on the official eVisa portal, evisacam.cm, and receives the visa on arrival or at an embassy.

faq.question: Does Cameroon offer a visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Not without prior approval. You must apply and be approved on evisacam.cm before traveling; the physical visa is then issued when you land at Douala, Yaoundé-Nsimalen or Garoua. Turning up with no eVisa approval risks being refused boarding or entry.

faq.question: How much does the Cameroon eVisa cost?
faq.answer: Roughly XAF 50,000 for a short-stay tourist visa and about double that for a long-stay visa, plus processing charges. The exact amount for your nationality and processing speed is shown during the evisacam.cm application.

faq.question: Is the yellow fever vaccine mandatory for Cameroon?
faq.answer: Yes — proof of yellow fever vaccination is required for all travelers aged 9 months and over, regardless of where you are arriving from, and the certificate is checked at the airport.

faq.question: Is Cameroon safe for tourists?
faq.answer: The main tourist areas — Douala, Yaoundé, Kribi and Limbe — see mostly trouble-free visits, but avoid the Northwest, Southwest and Far North regions, where armed conflict continues. Check your government's latest travel advice before booking.
